result: HBV infection represents a major global public health burden with 300 million chronic infections, 1.5 million new infections, and 1 million deaths annually, with uneven geographic distribution particularly affecting Africa and South East Asia.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C3, C7, and C8 are all supported by citations to authoritative sources (WHO, Cooke et al., O'Hara et al., Graber-Stiehl). The claims are internally consistent and represent well-established epidemiological data on HBV burden. These are descriptive epidemiological claims that establish the scope of the problem.

result: HBV disproportionately affects marginalized inclusion health populations (migrants, people experiencing homelessness, people who inject drugs, incarcerated individuals, sex workers, Roma and Traveller communities) whose needs are poorly met by existing healthcare systems, with only 10% of those infected being diagnosed.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C78, and C79 establish the core thesis of the manuscript linking HBV to inclusion health populations. All claims are supported by citations (O'Hara et al., Royal College of Physicians). The 10% diagnosis rate (C5) is a specific statistic that contextualizes the healthcare access problem. This represents the central argument of the review.

result: US funding for HIV research in 2022 is projected to be 20-fold greater than for HBV despite lower HIV prevalence.
evaluation: Claim C6 is supported by citation to National Institutes of Health 2022 data. This claim illustrates research funding disparities and contextualizes the relative neglect of HBV. The comparison is specific and quantified.

result: Migrants represent 3.6% of the global population (281 million), with approximately 90 million displaced by conflict. In Europe, migrants from intermediate/high HBV endemic countries have 5% HBV prevalence (10% in asylum seekers) compared to 1% in the general population.
evaluation: Claims C9-C14 provide epidemiological context for migrants and HBV prevalence. C9 and C11-C14 are supported by citations (International Organisation for Migration, ECDC, Kim et al.). C10 lacks a specific citation but is stated as factual knowledge. The prevalence comparisons are internally consistent and demonstrate elevated HBV burden in migrant populations.

result: Approximately 150 million people worldwide were homeless in 2020, with substantially increased all-cause mortality compared to housed populations and higher HBV seroprevalence.
evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by citations (Chamie 2017, Aldridge et al. 2018, Ly et al. 2021a). The claims establish the scale of homelessness globally and link it to both general mortality and HBV-specific outcomes. Table 2 is referenced for additional supporting data.

result: There are 15.6 million people who inject drugs and 283 million with alcohol use disorders globally. HBV disproportionately affects these populations, with alcohol increasing HBV transmission risk behaviors and acting synergistically with HBV to accelerate liver damage.
evaluation: Claims C18-C22 are supported by multiple citations (Degenhardt et al., WHO, Magri et al., Arasteh et al., Gitto et al., Li et al.). The claims establish population size, HBV burden, and mechanistic links between substance use and HBV outcomes. The synergistic effect of alcohol on liver damage (C22) is a specific pathophysiological claim supported by appropriate citations.

result: The global prison population is at least 10.77 million with 4.8% HBsAg prevalence. Twenty-five percent of PWID initiate drug use in prison, incarceration doubles the risk of re-initiating injection drug use, and frequency/duration of incarceration are positively associated with HBV prevalence.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by citations (Fair and Walmsley, Dolan et al., Nakitanda et al., Genberg et al., Kamarulzaman et al., Dana et al.). The claims establish prison population size, HBV prevalence, and specific risk factors linking incarceration to HBV transmission. The quantified associations are appropriately cited.

result: Sex workers are underrepresented in the literature with lacking robust data. Risk factors for HBV among commercial sex workers include older age, marital status, having children, fewer years of education, substance use, street-based work, and high client numbers.
evaluation: Claims C28 and C102 are supported by citations (Aldridge et al., Miranda et al., Matos et al., Todd et al.). C28 acknowledges a data gap, while C102 synthesizes available evidence on risk factors. The claims are consistent with the review's theme of underrepresentation of certain inclusion health populations.

result: Roma and Traveller populations in Europe number 10-12 million with 10-year lower life expectancy than the settled UK population. HBsAg prevalence is 9.4% in UK Roma and four-fold higher in Eastern Slovakia Roma compared to the general population, with risk factors including male sex, older age, tattoos, and imprisonment.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32 and C103 are supported by citations (Council of Europe, Equality and Human Rights Commission, Macejova et al., Gregory et al., Veselíny et al.). The claims establish population size, health disparities, HBV prevalence, and specific risk factors. The four-fold increased risk (C32) is a specific quantified finding.

result: Aboriginal Australians have higher HBV prevalence, liver disease rates, and poorer outcomes than non-Indigenous Australians. HBV genotype C4 is associated with aggressive disease progression and may have reduced vaccine efficacy. Indigenous populations globally face increased HBV burden and are poorly represented in data.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35 and C104-C105 are supported by citations (Plackett, Qama et al., Wigg et al., Davies et al., Einsiedel et al.). C34 notes that the impact of genotype C4 has not been separated from social determinants. C35 regarding vaccine efficacy is qualified as 'some evidence.' C105 is an inference synthesizing the section's findings. The claims appropriately acknowledge uncertainty while establishing the overall pattern.

result: Within inclusion health populations, females may experience worse HBV outcomes than males, contrasting with the general population where males have worse outcomes. Female migrants have twice the HBV infection risk, lower vaccination uptake, higher prevalence in pregnancy with late antenatal care, and dramatically elevated all-cause mortality (SMR 11.86 vs male SMR 7.88).
evaluation: Claims C36-C44, C106-C107 present evidence for sex-based differences in HBV outcomes within inclusion health populations. Most individual claims are supported by citations (Prestileo et al., Taylor et al., Tasa et al., Bierhoff et al., United Way Mumbai, Aldridge et al., Brown et al.). However, C107 explicitly states 'further work is needed to determine whether this sexual dimorphism is truly reversed,' indicating the authors themselves acknowledge uncertainty about the overall conclusion. The evidence is suggestive but not definitive.

result: Research on inclusion health and HBV is biased toward high-income settings (Europe/North America). Data collection in high-endemicity countries is hindered by criminalization/stigmatization of inclusion health populations. Available African data suggest intermediate-to-high HBV prevalence in CSWs, PWID, and incarcerated people, but HBV research, advocacy, and investment have been neglected in Africa.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 are supported by Table 2 reference and citations (Bitty-Anderson et al., Degenhardt et al., Dolan et al., Scheibe et al., Duby et al.). C109 and C112 are stated as factual knowledge claims about structural barriers and neglect. The claims establish geographic bias in the evidence base and identify Africa as a priority region with data gaps.

result: Major data gaps exist for HBV, exacerbated by COVID-19 pandemic, with worst impact in high-burden low-income settings. Good quality HBV data for inclusion health populations are lacking, mostly from small cross-sectional seroprevalence studies.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by citation (Pley et al.) and Table 2 reference. These claims identify methodological limitations in the existing evidence base and establish the need for better data collection. This is a critical assessment of the literature quality.

result: A safe, effective HBV vaccine has been available since 1982. WHO recommended universal birth dose vaccination in 2009, but coverage was only 42% globally (17% in WHO African Region) by 2021. Scaling up to >90% by 2030 would prevent 710,000 deaths. Vaccination prevented 310 million infections between 1990-2020.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 and C58 are supported by citations (WHO 2017, WHO 2022a, de Villiers et al., Cooke et al.). The claims establish vaccine availability, policy recommendations, current coverage gaps, and projected impact of improved coverage. The 710,000 deaths prevented (C49) is from modeling, appropriately cited. These claims establish the prevention context.

result: Only 25-35% of adults with chronic HBV are eligible for treatment under current guidelines, leaving the majority at risk. HBV/HIV co-infected individuals may have a treatment advantage due to greater access to early and consistent antiviral treatment.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by citations (McNaughton et al., Maponga et al.). C50 establishes treatment eligibility limitations under current guidelines. C51 identifies a paradoxical advantage for co-infected individuals, highlighting inequities in treatment access. These claims contextualize the treatment landscape.

result: Chronic HBV infection usually remains asymptomatic until late complications (fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC). There is no cure for HBV, but antivirals can suppress viral replication.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are stated as established medical knowledge without specific citations. These are well-established facts about HBV natural history and treatment that provide necessary background context. The lack of specific citations is appropriate for foundational medical knowledge.

result: HBV screening is cost-effective in various scenarios including community-based outreach and low-prevalence settings, largely due to averting costs of decompensated cirrhosis, HCC, and transplantation. ECDC recommends universal ED screening at >2% prevalence, but evidence suggests cost-effectiveness at >0.25%, leading to UK implementation.
evaluation: Claims C62, C64-C66 are supported by multiple citations (Su et al., Xiao et al., Toy et al., Nayagam et al., Tordrup et al., Hutton et al., Wright et al., Williams et al., Nebbia et al.). C63 is stated as an inference from the cost-effectiveness studies. C64 is stated as established ECDC policy. The claims establish the economic case for screening and identify policy implementation.

result: All pregnant women should be screened for HBV. Outreach screening services are feasible and acceptable. Community-based testing for migrants is effective with highest uptake when endorsed by local communities. Integrated infection screening in migrants is recommended, cost-effective, feasible, and acceptable.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by citations (WHO, CDC, O'Carroll et al., Carr et al., ECDC, Robotin and George, Seedat et al., Cinardo et al.). These claims establish evidence-based screening recommendations and implementation strategies. The claims synthesize guidance from authoritative sources.

result: Integrated infection screening is cost-effective. WHO's triple elimination initiative for HIV, syphilis, and HBV has reduced transmission rates, staff/patient time, and costs. Multi-morbidity is common in inclusion health populations, including high rates of co-infections and non-communicable diseases like cardiovascular disease and diabetes, which increases HBV-associated HCC risk.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by citations (WHO 2022b, Zhang et al., Ahmadi Gharaei et al., do Nascimento et al., La Torre et al., Al Shakarchi et al., Campbell et al.) except C52 which is stated as knowledge. The claims establish the rationale for integrated approaches and document the multi-morbidity burden. C57 provides a specific quantified risk (HR 1.36) for diabetes-HBV interaction.

result: A UK survey found many primary care practitioners did not believe routine HBV testing in migrants was necessary and national guidelines were poorly followed. Australian research identified lack of confidence and poor communication about HBV among healthcare professionals.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by citations (Evlampidou et al., Wallace et al., Robotin et al.). These claims identify healthcare provider knowledge gaps and implementation failures. This establishes the need for provider education and system-level interventions.

result: Peer-led approaches have been successful in HIV, TB, and HCV. The HepCare project demonstrated that people with lived experience can be upskilled as equal healthcare team members, providing cost-effective enhancement of diagnosis, linkage to care, and treatment success. People with lived experience ranked peer-led advocacy as the second most important intervention after stable housing.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 and C91-C92 are supported by citations (Ward et al., Surey et al., Luchenski et al., Paisi et al., Crone et al., Story et al., Øgård-Repål et al.). The claims establish evidence for peer-led interventions and their prioritization by affected communities. The HepCare example (C74) provides a specific successful model.

result: Viral hepatitis is recognized as a global health priority within UN SDG 2030, with targets including 90% HBV vaccine coverage, 90% reduction in new chronic infections and new infections, and 65% reduction in attributable mortality.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by citation (Cooke et al.) and stated as established UN policy. These claims establish the global policy framework and elimination targets that contextualize the manuscript's recommendations.

result: Inclusion health populations face multiple intersecting barriers to HBV care including: forced relocation disrupting continuity of care, overlapping risk factors (homelessness, incarceration, substance use), stigma and discrimination, competing priorities for basic needs, co-morbidities, lack of disclosure to providers, cultural and structural barriers, and inadequate funding for harm reduction programs.
evaluation: Claims C80-C98 are supported by numerous citations documenting specific barriers across different inclusion health populations. The claims establish the complex, intersecting nature of barriers to care. C97 lacks a specific citation but is stated as factual knowledge. The evidence converges to support the overall conclusion about systemic barriers.

result: Published HBV literature on prisons consists mainly of small cross-sectional studies that don't reflect dynamic prison populations. Prisons act as 'concentration mechanisms' for infectious disease amplification and dissemination through multiple HBV transmission routes including needle sharing, unsterile tattooing, and high-risk sexual activity.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by citations (Wirtz et al., Dolan et al., Kamarulzaman et al., Moazen et al., Kowo et al., Harawa et al.). C99 critiques the existing literature quality. C100-C101 establish the mechanistic basis for elevated HBV risk in prison settings. The 'concentration mechanism' concept is appropriately attributed.

result: Point-of-care HBsAg tests enable community-based diagnosis, though global efforts are needed to ensure regular supply in resource-constrained settings. Active targeted screening efforts are an important step toward HBV elimination.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by citations (Lemoine et al., ECDC). The claims establish the availability of diagnostic tools and identify implementation challenges in resource-limited settings. This connects diagnostic technology to elimination strategies.
